_howTo: Radio talks with Walla Walla. Each talk has turns; in each turn Walla Walla says "them" and the player picks one of up to three "replies". A reply can have a "back" line, and "right": true marks the right answer to a question (it is never scored). Every reply leads on to the next turn. "cue" is when the talk comes on: "start" as the lesson opens, {"after": "<figure>"} once that figure's task is done, or "check" as the final check opens. "locals" names who in town asked a forecast question, by the forecast's "id" in the lesson file.

turns.them: Harrow, Walla Walla. I hear the Sunday school has your answer pinned to the wall. Miss Abernathy says you’re nearly as reliable as the almanac.

replies.back: The almanac has been wrong for longer. That earns a certain respect.

turns.them: Harvest is coming. Ole Haugen has the binder out in the wheat, and cut wheat can’t sit wet. He wants to know how much warning he’ll get before rain. And Hap Delaney came on the air from Pasco: he has the afternoon mail run, and he wants to know how to tell from the morning sky whether he’ll be flying into rain by afternoon.

replies.say: How much warning can anybody get?
replies.back: A day, sometimes more, if you look up high. The ice clouds out in front tell you what’s coming long before it gets here.

replies.say: Hap could just look out the window.
replies.back: Hap looks out the window plenty. He just doesn’t know what he’s looking at.

turns.them: This week: the high floor, all ice, and the grey sheets that come down after it. And a ring around the sun that’s older than Aunt Fern’s knee.

replies.say: Nothing is older than Aunt Fern’s knee.
replies.back: Don’t tell her I said so.

turns.them: You’ve got your ring. Hold your hand out at arm’s length: about how far is it from the sun to the ring?

replies.back: Twenty-two degrees, a spread hand at arm’s length. Every halo, every time. Ice crystals don’t bend the rules, only the light.
Much bigger than that. Twenty-two degrees is a whole spread hand at arm’s length.
That’s the beauty of it: it never does. The crystals bend the light by the same 22 degrees every time.

turns.them: Aunt Fern says a ring around the moon means rain soon. For once she has science on her side. Don’t tell her that either.

replies.say: Even a knee is right sometimes.

turns.them: Now, Ole’s question. A warm front is on its way. In what order do its clouds arrive?

replies.say: High clouds first, then middle, then low.
replies.back: Top down, like a lid closing. Each step means the front is that much closer.
Backwards. The warm air slides up over the cold along a long, gentle slope, so the highest clouds arrive first, far out ahead.
Then nobody would get any warning and Ole would lose his wheat. High first, then middle, then low.

turns.them: Now you can give Ole a timetable instead of a shrug.

replies.back: Except this one runs on time.

turns.them: The club’s photographs are done. Now Ole and Hap. Harvest and the mail: the two things this county can’t do without.

replies.back: Ask Ole and he’ll say wheat. Ask Hap and he’ll say the mail. Ask Mabel and she’ll say the gossip in the mail.
